Answer any SIX questions. All questions carry 17 marks each. For your guidance, the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You will be graded on your ability to use good English, organise information clearly and the use of specialist vocabulary where appropriate. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) State the functions of a graphic card in a computer. (2 marks)

(b) Explain the role of firmware in a system. (2 marks)

(c) Describe a device controller and give one example. (2 marks)

(a) Give two functions of the operating system. (2 marks)

(b) Explain pre-emptive and non-pre-emptive scheduling methods. (2 marks)

(c) State one property of each of command line and graphic user interfaces. Give an example of each of the interfaces. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Two functions of the operating system (2 marks)** (any two):

- **Process (task) management and scheduling:** decides which program uses the processor and when.
- **Memory management:** allocates main memory to programs and frees it when they end.
- **File management:** creates, stores, names, protects and retrieves files and folders.
- **Device management:** controls input/output devices through device drivers.
- **Providing the user interface** and **security** (user accounts, passwords, access rights).

**(b) Pre-emptive and non-pre-emptive scheduling (2 marks).**

- In **pre-emptive scheduling** the operating system **can interrupt a running process and take the processor away from it** before it has finished (for example when its time slice ends or when a higher-priority process arrives), and give it to another process. Examples: Round Robin, shortest remaining time first.
- In **non-pre-emptive scheduling** a process **keeps the processor until it finishes or waits for input/output**; it cannot be interrupted by the scheduler. Examples: First Come First Served, Shortest Job First.

**(c) Command line interface (CLI) and graphical user interface (GUI) (3 marks).**

| Interface | One property | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Command line | The user **types text commands** and must know the commands and their syntax; it uses little memory and is fast and powerful for experienced users. | MS-DOS, Windows Command Prompt, Linux terminal |
| Graphical user interface | The user works with **windows, icons, menus and a pointer (mouse or touch)**, which is easy to learn and use but needs more memory and processing power. | Microsoft Windows, macOS, Android |

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Describe a relational database. (2 marks)

(b) Differentiate between data redundancy and data integrity. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(a) Relational database (2 marks).** A relational database stores data in **several tables (relations)**. Each table is made of **rows (records or tuples) and columns (fields or attributes)**, and each record is identified by a **primary key**. The tables are **linked to each other through relationships**, using a field that is the primary key in one table and a foreign key in another, so that data are stored once and combined when needed. The data are managed and queried with SQL. Examples of systems: MySQL, Oracle, Microsoft Access.

**(b) Data redundancy and data integrity (2 marks).**

| | Data redundancy | Data integrity |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | The **unnecessary repetition (duplication) of the same data** in several places in a file or database. | The **accuracy, consistency and reliability** of data throughout their life, so that they stay correct and valid. |
| Effect | Wastes storage space and leads to inconsistency (one copy is updated, another is not). | Data can be trusted; it is protected by validation rules, keys and constraints. |
| Aim | To be **reduced** (for example by normalisation). | To be **maintained**; redundancy that is not controlled threatens it. |
